articles.body: Originally published at ictcrm.com Italy's data protection authority has fined BBVA €5,508,000 because one customer's marketing opt-out never reached the system that sent the marketing. The choice was recorded, a sync between internal systems and the CRM unit failed, and promotions kept arriving for seven months. If your CRM software holds consent in one place and sends from another, this is the case to read. The European Data Protection Board published the summary of the decision on 9 October 2026. The Garante, Italy's regulator, made the final decision on 3 July 2026. Three days after the BBVA summary, the EDPB published a second Italian decision, a €16.7 million fine against the telecoms operator Wind Tre, which turns on the same failure at a much larger scale.

articles.title: Day 1: I'm building a secure text editor with Electron in public
articles.excerpt: I often feel like everyone around me is ahead, so I’m doing something about it: 30 days, one project, built in public. I’m learning Node.js, Express and Electron by making simple projects, for starter…
articles.body: I often feel like everyone around me is ahead, so I’m doing something about it: 30 days, one project, built in public . I’m learning Node.js, Express and Electron by making simple projects, for starters a simple mini text editor. Day 1: a window that opens. It’s an empty dark window right now, but it’s mine. I customized the background, edited index.html. What I learned: Electron has two sides. main.js runs in Node and creates the window. index.html is just a web page that the window displays. I didn’t understand this split until I saw it work. What confused me: I didn’t understand how index.html connects to everything else and how it all works together. Here’s how I understand it now: main.js creates the window and loads index.html with win.loadFile('index.html').

articles.title: Beyond Software Recovery: How to Verify Industrial Equipment Before Restarting
articles.excerpt: A system can be online, its software restored, and its network connections working again—yet the equipment it controls may still not be ready to operate. This is a key challenge in industrial cybersec…
articles.body: A system can be online, its software restored, and its network connections working again—yet the equipment it controls may still not be ready to operate. This is a key challenge in industrial cybersecurity. Unlike conventional IT systems, industrial systems connect digital decisions to physical actions. A robot may move during a communication outage, a vehicle's load condition may change, or a drone may lose reliable mission-state information. After a cybersecurity incident, restoring software is only part of the recovery process. Teams also need to establish whether the digital system accurately represents the equipment's current condition and whether commands can be trusted. The goal is not simply to bring a system back online.

articles.title: How Can a Program Produce Different Results Every Time You Run It?
articles.excerpt: Have you ever written a program that works perfectly on one run but produces a completely different result the next time? You change nothing, use the same input, and somehow the output is different. A…
articles.body: Have you ever written a program that works perfectly on one run but produces a completely different result the next time? You change nothing, use the same input, and somehow the output is different. At first, it might seem like a compiler issue, a hardware problem, or a bug that appears out of nowhere. In many cases, however, the reason is much more fundamental: the program depends on the order in which multiple operations execute, and that order is not guaranteed. This behavior is closely related to concurrency, thread scheduling, shared state, and race conditions. Understanding these concepts is important because they can explain some of the most frustrating bugs in software development. 1.

articles.title: The Edge-Computing Shift: Architecting Middleware Security and Scaling Strategies
articles.excerpt: Originally published on tamiz.pro. The shift to edge-computing is not merely a matter of moving code closer to the user; it is a fundamental reimagining of where logic resides and how it secures itsel…
articles.body: Originally published on tamiz.pro . The Distributed Dilemma The shift to edge-computing is not merely a matter of moving code closer to the user; it is a fundamental reimagining of where logic resides and how it secures itself. As workloads migrate to the perimeter, the traditional centralized security model—where a firewall protects the perimeter of a data center—becomes obsolete. In an edge-computing environment, the perimeter is effectively everywhere, meaning that every node, container, and function must be treated as a potential threat. This article explores the specific architectural challenges of middleware in this context, focusing on how to implement robust security controls and scaling mechanisms without sacrificing the low-latency benefits that define the edge. 1.

articles.title: NASA's SkyFall helicopters will 'show us parts of Mars we've never seen before', scientists say
articles.excerpt: "Just like here on Earth, Mars helicopters can cover distance quickly and can go places that might be impossible to reach by ground."
articles.body: NASA is accelerating the development of three helicopters that will be deployed into the sky above Mars after a voyage aboard NASA's Space Reactor‑1 Freedom spacecraft. Slated for launch in 2028, SR-1 Freedom is the first fission nuclear-powered interplanetary spacecraft and is assigned the duty of dropping off the SkyFall entry capsule loaded with the trio of aerial vehicles at the Red Planet. SR-1's trajectory will deliver the SkyFall helicopters in Mars' northern hemisphere during the planet's spring season to avoid dust storms . SkyFall is based on the success of the first aerial craft to float about the Red Planet , Ingenuity , which flew over 70 missions at Jezero Crater before it finally broke a rotor . It was designed to fly five.

articles.title: Windblown yardangs on Mars | Space photo of the day for Oct. 15, 2026
articles.excerpt: Martian sands blown by strong winds left rippled ridges on the surface of the Red Planet, as seen in this new image from the Mars Express spacecraft.
articles.body: A new image from the Mars Express spacecraft reveals windblown ridges known as yardangs, seen here as wrinkled sections on the left and right sides of the image. (Image credit: ESA/DLR/FU Berlin) A new image from the European Space Agency's Mars Express spacecraft reveals the powerful erosive forces that have shaped and re-shaped the surface of the Red Planet over long periods of geological time. What is it? This new Mars Express image captures Amazonis Mensa, a large, flat mountain on the Red Planet that offers planetary scientists a glimpse into the many factors that can sculpt a world's surface. In this photograph, several features stand out to help illustrate this. Easiest to make out are the large round craters created by ancient impacts on the surface of Mars .

articles.title: Beat light pollution with these six portable telescopes
articles.excerpt: Sick of skyglow spoiling your stargazing? These six telescopes are portable enough that you can easily pack them away and seek out darker skies.
articles.body: Light pollution is the astronomer's biggest enemy, especially if you're gazing into deep space. And while some of the best telescopes can make a difference, there's no way to eliminate it. That's why, if you want to observe the cosmos without obstruction, you need to seek out darker skies, get a smart telescope or combine the two. You don't have to book a flight to a dark sky reserve ; just traveling away from suburbia can be enough. That's where portable telescopes come in. Set one up in a field, for example, and you'll get a vastly improved view of the cosmos. Galaxies, nebulas and other deep space objects become more detailed when they're not washed out by skyglow.
